title: Matrix Calculus for Gradients
summary: Gradients and Jacobians of vector/matrix functions — exactly enough to read a backprop derivation without re-deriving deep learning itself.

slides.markdown:
Scalar calculus gives you `d(loss)/d(one number)`. But a model has thousands of weights — you need `d(loss)/d(every weight at once)`. **Matrix calculus** is scalar calculus generalized to vectors and matrices, one level up.

You don't need to re-derive it from scratch; you need to recognize the handful of identities that every backprop derivation reuses.

- The **gradient** generalizes a derivative to a vector input.
- The **Jacobian** generalizes it further, to a vector *output*.
- A small set of identities (`∇(Ax)`, `∇(xᵀAx)`) covers most of what shows up in ML derivations.

slides.subTitle: Shape conventions
slides.markdown:
For a scalar function `f(x)` of a vector `x` (size `n`), the **gradient** `∇f` is a vector of the same size `n` — one partial derivative per input coordinate: `∇f = [∂f/∂x1, ..., ∂f/∂xn]`.

The convention worth memorizing: **the gradient always matches the shape of the input it's taken with respect to.** If `x` is `n x 1`, `∇f` is `n x 1` too — this single rule catches most shape-mismatch bugs before you even compute anything.

Gradient descent then just moves `x` a small step in the direction `-∇f` — downhill.

slides.subTitle: A cheat-sheet
slides.markdown:
Three identities cover the bulk of ML gradient derivations:

| Function | Gradient |
|---|---|
| `f(x) = aᵀx` (linear) | `∇f = a` |
| `f(x) = xᵀAx` (quadratic form) | `∇f = (A + Aᵀ)x`, or `2Ax` if `A` symmetric |
| `f(x) = \|\|Ax - b\|\|²` (squared error) | `∇f = 2Aᵀ(Ax - b)` |

Memorize these three and you can read almost any ML loss-gradient derivation without re-deriving from first principles each time.

slides.subTitle: The Jacobian matrix
slides.markdown:
When a function outputs a **vector**, not a scalar (e.g. a neural net layer producing 128 activations from 64 inputs), the derivative generalizes further to the **Jacobian**: a matrix `J` where `J[i][j] = ∂(output_i)/∂(input_j)`.

Shape rule: if the output is size `m` and input is size `n`, the Jacobian is `m x n` — every output-input pair gets its own entry.

The gradient is just a special case of the Jacobian where the output happens to be a single scalar (`m=1`).

slides.subTitle: Chain rule in matrix form
slides.markdown:
For composed layers `y = f(g(x))`, the chain rule becomes a **matrix product** of Jacobians: `J_y = J_f · J_g`. Each layer contributes its local Jacobian; the full gradient is their product, layer by layer.

This is exactly what **backpropagation** computes (Area 12 `deep-learning`): the loss gradient w.r.t. an early layer's weights is the product of every Jacobian between that layer and the loss, computed right-to-left.

Order matters here too — matrix multiplication isn't commutative, so composition order must match the network's layer order.

slides.subTitle: Gradient of squared error loss
slides.markdown:
Linear model loss: `L(w) = ||Xw - y||²`. Applying the squared-error identity from the cheat-sheet directly:

```
L(w) = (Xw - y)ᵀ(Xw - y)
∇L   = 2Xᵀ(Xw - y)
```

Setting `∇L = 0` and solving for `w` recovers exactly the normal equations `XᵀXw = Xᵀy` from linear regression — matrix calculus is how that formula is actually derived, not just asserted.

slides.subTitle: Shape mismatches
slides.markdown:
The single most common bug in hand-written gradient code is a **shape mismatch** — something mathematically close but transposed or wrongly-dimensioned, silently producing nonsense instead of an error.

The fix habit: before trusting any gradient formula, check its output shape matches the shape of the variable you're differentiating with respect to. `∇f` must always match `x`'s shape — mismatch means a transpose bug, not a subtle math error.

This one check catches most "my backprop gives garbage" bugs before you even run the code.

slides.subTitle: Gradient of softmax cross-entropy
slides.markdown:
Softmax converts logits `z` to probabilities `p = softmax(z)`, and cross-entropy loss `L = -Σ y_i log(p_i)` compares `p` to a one-hot label `y`. Deriving `∂L/∂z` by hand (product rule through softmax) looks intimidating — but the two steps' derivatives cancel into one of the cleanest results in ML:

```
∂L/∂z = p - y
```

The gradient w.r.t. each logit is simply "predicted probability minus true label" — for the correct class it's `p_correct - 1` (negative, push logit up), for every wrong class it's `p_wrong - 0 = p_wrong` (positive, push logit down). This is exactly why softmax + cross-entropy is the default classification pairing: the combined gradient is this simple only because the two functions' derivatives are chosen to cancel.

slides.subTitle: Numerator vs denominator layout
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "there's one correct shape for a Jacobian, so any gradient library or textbook formula should match mine directly." **Why it's wrong:** matrix calculus has two competing conventions — **numerator layout** (Jacobian shaped by the output) and **denominator layout** (shaped by the input) — and they produce *transposed* versions of each other.

A formula copied from a paper using one convention, plugged into code written against the other, silently transposes your gradient — no error thrown, just wrong numbers propagating through training.

**Correct model:** before trusting a formula from an unfamiliar source, check which layout it uses (usually stated near the notation section), and verify a small example by hand against your library's actual output shape.
